item.title: Forg365 Microsoft 365 Phishing, Russian Coms Charges, and EU GRU Sanctions
item.content:encoded:
Forg365 PhaaS Targets Microsoft 365 with Device Code and AitM Session Theft — Should Read

Forg365 is a Telegram-sold phishing-as-a-service platform targeting Microsoft 365 with device code phishing, adversary-in-the-middle session theft, antibot evasion, and tools to maintain access and operate inside compromised mailboxes. The key defense is to restrict device code authentication and closely audit mailbox activity, mail rules, tokens, and legacy forwarding aliases.

  • Forg365 is a phishing-as-a-service operation sold via Telegram for $400 per month or $3,800 per year and targets Microsoft 365 accounts.
  • Forg365 attack chains use phishing lures delivered through legitimate email infrastructure such as Amazon SES and Twilio SendGrid before redirecting victims to Forg365-controlled domains.
  • The platform supports device code phishing that shows a Microsoft-styled verification code page and pushes victims into a legitimate Microsoft Authentication Broker sign-in flow that authorizes an attacker-controlled session.
  • Forg365 includes a Chromium browser extension called ForgCookie that is designed to maintain access to compromised Microsoft accounts by generating and injecting refresh-token credential cookies and capturing Microsoft cookies.
  • The platform supports post-compromise mailbox operations such as monitoring compromised email accounts for specific keywords and using AI assistance to draft replies in email threads.

EU sanctions Russian GRU military hackers over cyberattacks — Should Read

The EU and UK sanctioned Russian GRU officers, FSB-linked hackers, cybercriminals, and related entities accused of coordinating cyberattacks, espionage, influence operations, and critical infrastructure targeting across Europe. Officials specifically linked Russian groups including Turla and Sandworm to campaigns against government, defense, energy, and nuclear research targets, including failed attacks in Poland.

  • The European Union sanctioned nine individuals and four entities, including Russian GRU officers and cybercriminals, over malicious cyber activity targeting the EU, its member states, and international partners.
  • The United Kingdom separately sanctioned 24 individuals and entities, including senior GRU figures Vyacheslav Stafeyev, Ivan Senin, and Ivan Kasyanenko, whom officials said directed cyber and hybrid operations.
  • The Council of the EU publicly identified the 16th Centre of Russia's Federal Security Service as controlling several cyber threat groups, including Turla.
  • Officials said the FSB-linked unit has targeted government networks and critical infrastructure in multiple European countries and conducted cyberespionage against government and defense targets since 2010.
  • The article says Russian-linked hackers were connected to failed attacks on Polish critical infrastructure, including a late-December incident affecting dozens of power grid entities and another blocked attack against Poland's National Centre for Nuclear Research.

Attacker Uses Suspected AI-Generated PowerShell Script to Map Active Directory — Should Read

Huntress observed an intruder using a likely AI-generated PowerShell script to aggressively enumerate Active Directory after gaining RDP access with stolen credentials, then exfiltrating the results. The key takeaway is that AI is helping lower-skilled attackers execute familiar intrusion playbooks faster and at greater scale, even without novel malware or zero-days.

  • Huntress reported an early June 2026 intrusion in which an unknown threat actor used pre-compromised credentials to gain RDP access to a domain-joined Windows Server.
  • The attacker staged tools in C:\ProgramData\ and used a suspected AI-generated PowerShell script to locate the Domain Controller and enumerate Active Directory users, computers, groups, organizational units, and trusts.
  • Huntress said the PowerShell script showed signs of AI generation, including a prompt-like title, placeholder strings, over-engineered fallback methods, and beautified console output.
  • About 30 minutes after the Active Directory enumeration, the attacker deployed s5cmd and SharpShares to search for user-accessible data repositories.
  • Sygnia separately reported an AI-assisted cloud attack against a large AWS-based environment that moved from initial access to broad compromise in about 72 hours using familiar cloud techniques rather than novel malware or zero-days.

Authenticated at Delivery, Forged at Origin — Should Read

A phishing email that failed SPF and DMARC at its origin was made to look legitimate after mailbox auto-forwarding gave it aligned authentication and ARC preserved the new pass verdict. Defenders should inspect the full Received chain and decoded redirect path, not trust final DMARC results or trusted-domain links alone.

  • A fake eSignature notification with the subject “AgreementDOC-79488 Is Ready For You” reached a Canadian legal advocacy organization’s reporting inbox with DKIM pass, DMARC pass, and compauth pass at delivery.
  • At the first hop, Microsoft recorded the message from 188[.]215[.]229[.]105 on v519eu[.]mailgun[.]net as SPF fail, DMARC fail, and DKIM none because the sending host was not authorized for the From domain.
  • An ordinary mailbox auto-forward gave the message a fresh envelope sender aligned to the forwarding organization, after which subsequent Microsoft hops sealed the authentication results into an Authenticated Received Chain.
  • The message body used a repurposed-looking corporate legal thread to support a single call to action labeled “Your Secured documents are ready. View Document Here.”
  • The call-to-action link began with a Google open redirect, passed through an ad-click redirect on adservice[.]google[.]com[.]ar, and landed on ruslanstudio[.]com, a domain registered in 2022 to a registrant in Lalitpur, Nepal.

UK charges suspects linked to Russian Coms call spoofing platform — Should Read

UK authorities charged five London suspects linked to Russian Coms, a caller ID spoofing platform used to make over 1.8 million scam calls by impersonating banks, telecoms, and law enforcement. The platform has been tied to tens of millions in losses and an estimated 170,000 victims worldwide.

  • UK authorities charged five London residents following a National Crime Agency investigation into Russian Coms, a caller ID spoofing platform used by criminals to make over 1.8 million scam calls.
  • The charges include conspiracy to supply articles for use in connection with fraud, transferring or converting criminal property, and, for Zakkaria Sehailia, failing to comply with a notice to provide phone passcodes.
  • Russian Coms allowed criminals to hide their identity by making calls appear to come from pre-selected numbers belonging to financial institutions, telecommunications companies, and law enforcement agencies.
  • Since 2020, Russian Coms has been linked to tens of millions in financial losses affecting an estimated 170,000 victims.
  • The NCA said criminals used the platform to call 500,000 unique phone numbers across more than 107 countries before it was shut down.

Meta Files Patent for AI That Can Listen All Day and Track How You're Feeling — May Read

Meta has filed a patent for an AI system that could listen to users throughout the day, infer emotions from voice and other signals like eye tracking and phone activity, and log those readings with time and context. The idea is not a product yet, but it raises major privacy and regulatory concerns around always-on emotion tracking.

  • Meta filed patent application US 2026/0182881 for an AI system that can record speech across the day, infer emotional state from words and vocal cues, and keep timestamped logs tied to context such as time, location, activity, and phone use.
  • The filing says the system could run on devices including smart glasses, phones, smartwatches, headphones, or smart home speakers, with some versions listening all day and others checking only at set times.
  • The patent describes using additional signals beyond voice, including pupil size, blink rate, eye moisture, viewed or liked posts, screen time, and app-switching speed, to build an emotional profile.
  • The application also describes a real-time fitness coach that uses smart glasses to monitor workout form and adjust coaching based on the user's inferred mood.
  • The article states that Meta has not announced a product based on the filing, and notes that EU AI Act rules already ban emotion-inference AI in workplaces and schools except for medical or safety reasons.

Introducing Precursor: detecting agentic behavior with continuous client-side signals — Optional

Cloudflare launched Precursor, a client-side, session-based bot detection system that continuously analyzes behavioral signals across a user’s journey to better distinguish humans from automated agents. It integrates with Cloudflare Bot Management and Turnstile to improve bot scoring while reducing unnecessary challenges for legitimate users.

  • Cloudflare introduced Precursor, a client-side, session-based verification system that uses dynamically injected JavaScript to continuously collect behavioral signals as visitors interact with an application.
  • Precursor is an optional complement to Cloudflare Turnstile and is available as part of Cloudflare Enterprise Bot Management.
  • The system collects signals such as pointer movement, keyboard activity, focus changes, and visibility, then sends buffered data to an edge evaluation layer for analysis.
  • Precursor evaluates behavior across an entire session so automated activity cannot reset its behavioral signature simply by refreshing the page or starting over with a new challenge.
  • Cloudflare says Precursor is designed with privacy in mind by collecting minimum behavioral information, such as keyboard timing and rhythm rather than actual keys pressed, and by consuming signals internally rather than exposing them in customer dashboards.

Rust-proof your code with our new Testing Handbook chapter — Optional

Trail of Bits added a new Rust chapter to its Testing Handbook covering security testing tools, review gotchas, memory zeroization, dependency vetting, and specialized testing like Miri, Clippy, proptest, and Kani. It also released rust-review, a Claude Code plugin for automated Rust security reviews.

  • Trail of Bits added a new chapter to its Testing Handbook that provides a comprehensive guide to security testing Rust programs.
  • The chapter covers Rust security guarantees and limitations, including unwind safety, nondeterminism, and arithmetic errors.
  • The chapter describes dynamic and static analysis tools and techniques, including Miri, proptest, coverage measurement, mutation testing, and Clippy.
  • The chapter includes guidance for manual Rust code reviews, including gotchas and footguns, operator precedence issues, and memory zeroization approaches.
  • Trail of Bits released rust-review, a Claude Code plugin co-built with Aptos Labs for automated Rust security reviews across more than a dozen bug classes.

Thinking Fast and Slow in the SOC: The Case for Combining Autonomous AI with Analyst Copilots — Optional

The article argues that effective SOC AI should mirror human “fast and slow” thinking: autonomous systems should triage and investigate nearly all alerts at scale, while analyst copilots and humans focus only on the small percentage of cases requiring judgment. Without this split, teams either burn out on manual triage or misuse expensive frontier AI on raw alert queues without solving coverage gaps.

  • The article compares SOC decision-making to Daniel Kahneman’s System 1 and System 2 model, arguing that most alerts need fast, automatic processing while a small minority need deliberate human judgment.
  • Research cited in the article says 98% of enterprise alerts can be resolved autonomously, while less than 2% warrant human review.
  • The article argues that forcing human analysts to manually triage large alert volumes exhausts their capacity and can leave real threats hidden in low-severity alerts.
  • The article says frontier AI tools such as Claude, Codex, and Cursor are best used for escalated cases, detection rule engineering, incident reporting, and threat hunting rather than raw alert triage at full scale.
  • The article argues that enterprises using MDR providers may not own the accumulated investigation knowledge layer needed to make analyst copilots useful.

13th July – Threat Intelligence Report — Optional

This week’s threat intelligence roundup highlights major data breaches, emerging AI-enabled attack risks, and critical vulnerabilities affecting routers, Linux KVM, U-Boot, and Opera GX. It also tracks active threat groups including Cavern Manticore, ShinyHunters, JadePuffer, and UAT-7810 targeting government, cloud, crypto, and networking ecosystems.

  • AssuranceAmerica disclosed a data breach affecting approximately 7 million people after attackers used compromised employee credentials to access company systems and steal personal, insurance, vehicle, and claims information.
  • Latvijas Valsts Meži suffered a ransomware attack that disrupted mapping, hunting, contractor, and customer systems after attackers exploited a system that had remained unpatched for two years and leaked about 44GB of internal data.
  • Injective Labs experienced a supply chain compromise in which attackers accessed its SDK project and published malicious npm packages that exfiltrated cryptocurrency wallet private keys and seed phrases.
  • Researchers profiled JadePuffer, an autonomous ransomware operation that used a large language model to exploit CVE-2025-3248 in an exposed Langflow instance, access a production MySQL server, exfiltrate data, delete the database, and issue an extortion demand.
  • Several significant vulnerabilities were reported or patched, including a Tenda router authentication backdoor, a Linux KVM flaw that could allow a malicious guest virtual machine to corrupt host memory, U-Boot secure boot verification flaws, and an Opera GX issue allowing malicious browser modifications.
